name: Tulpamaxxing

card.summary: Tulpamaxxing is the practice of deliberately creating a 'tulpa', an imagined companion, through meditation and visualisation, which some forum users describe as a way to build a mental study partner or thinking aid.
card.note: Extended practice has been linked in forum accounts to sleep loss and distressing dissociative experiences.

quick.overview:
Tulpamaxxing applies the self-improvement vocabulary of looksmaxxing to tulpamancy, the practice of cultivating a willed imaginary companion. In forum posts, the goal is mental optimisation: a tulpa imagined as a study partner or a 'ChatGPT in my head' that could help its creator think and learn.

The idea comes from the wider tulpa subculture, which borrows a Tibetan Buddhist-derived term. Survey research on tulpa creators exists, mostly from the broader community, while the 'maxxing' framing is documented mainly through forum threads.
quick.how: Practitioners in the wider tulpa community describe sustained meditation, visualisation and regular 'conversation' with the imagined companion over months. One looksmax.org user described setting out the traits he wanted his tulpa to have on day one and continuing for about a year.
quick.risks: Researchers have reported that tulpa creators show higher hallucination proneness than comparison groups. One looksmax.org user described a year of practice ending in several days without sleep and distressing experiences; he linked his state to other substances as well. People with a history of dissociation or psychosis are generally advised by clinicians to be cautious with such practices.

lead: Tulpamaxxing is a term used on looksmax.org for creating a tulpa, a deliberately cultivated imaginary companion, as a form of mental optimisation [1]. It sits at the edge of the looksmaxxing vocabulary: rather than changing appearance directly, it aims to improve thinking and study, which proponents see as part of overall self-improvement.

The word tulpa comes from the Tibetan sprul pa and was reshaped by early twentieth-century Western theosophists and writers into the idea of a being produced by concentrated thought. Modern online practitioners, called tulpamancers, usually treat tulpas as psychological rather than paranormal phenomena [2].

In the one looksmax.org thread on the subject, a user described starting a tulpa as a joke that became a project meant to make him 'the smartest person in the world', specifying that it would function as a study aid in his head [1].

chain: Create an imagined companion through meditation
Use it as a study and thinking partner
Claimed gains in learning and focus
angle.text: Proponents frame a tulpa as an internal study partner that could sharpen thinking and learning. Any benefit to appearance would be indirect, through confidence or productivity, and is not documented.

paras: A tulpa, in modern usage, is a willed imaginary friend that its creator regards as relatively independent and sentient. Practitioners generally describe building it through concentration, visualisation and regular imagined dialogue [2]. Tulpamaxxing adds a goal of using the companion for self-improvement, as in the looksmax.org user's plan for a study-focused tulpa [1].

The Tibetan term was taken up by Western theosophists such as Annie Besant, whose 1905 Thought-Forms catalogued thought-forms, and later by Alexandra David-Néel, who claimed to have created and then dissolved a tulpa in the 1920s while acknowledging she might have been hallucinating [2]. Online tulpamancy communities grew on 4chan and Reddit and later Discord, helped by discussion among adult fans of My Little Pony [2].

Anthropologist Samuel Veissière's surveys found respondents were mostly young, urban and Euro-American, with many citing loneliness or social anxiety; 93.7 percent said tulpa involvement had improved their condition, and 76.5 percent preferred neurological or psychological explanations [2]. A 2022 study linked tulpamancy and ASMR experiences to hallucination proneness [2].

The looksmax.org thread titled around a 'tulpamaxxing experiment gone wrong' describes about a year of practice, days without sleep and the poster's fear of developing a dissociative disorder or psychosis; he also mentions drug use [1]. It is a single anecdotal account.
No studies found. Survey research has examined the broader tulpa community, not tulpamaxxing as a self-improvement method [2].

timeline.event: Alexandra David-Néel reports creating a tulpa in Tibet [2]

lore.intro: Tulpamaxxing appears on looksmax.org as a fringe mental-optimisation idea, with one prominent thread in which a user reports distressing results [1].

claims.claim: A tulpa can act as a built-in study partner that makes you smarter
claims.believers: The thread's author began with the stated aim of a tulpa that would study like 'a ChatGPT thing' in his head [1].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested tulpa creation as a cognitive aid; survey research reports self-rated improvements in mood and loneliness [2].

claims.claim: Long tulpa practice can produce lasting distress
claims.believers: One user reported sleeplessness and unfamiliar posts on his account after a year [1].
claims.experts: Studies link tulpamancy with higher hallucination proneness, without establishing cause [2].
